headline: India-UK Trade Pact Takes Effect, Slashing Tariffs on Thousands of Goods
subheadline: The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, the most sweeping trade deal New Delhi has signed, came into force on July 15, eliminating duties on 99% of Indian exports to Britain and opening services access across 137 sub-sectors.
body:
• Britain immediately removes duties on 96.8% of tariff lines, covering 97.7% of trade by value; Indian textiles, leather, gems, marine products and processed foods enter duty-free.
  • India eliminates tariffs on 64.1% of lines at once and phases out duties on a further 21%, while shielding sensitive agricultural products.
  • A linked social security agreement exempts roughly 75,000 Indian professionals and 900 employers from double National Insurance contributions for up to five years.
  • The deal is India's sixth FTA under the Modi government, following Mauritius, UAE, Australia, EFTA and Oman.

India and Britain's Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement came into force on July 15, cutting tariffs on thousands of goods and expanding market access for services firms and professionals in both countries. The pact, concluded after fourteen rounds of negotiations and signed on July 24, 2025, spans thirty chapters covering goods, services, digital trade and—for the first time in an Indian bilateral deal—government procurement.

India exported $13.44 billion of goods to Britain and imported $11.68 billion in the 2025/26 fiscal year. Bilateral services trade totalled $35.44 billion in 2024, with India running a services surplus of nearly $7.9 billion, according to Indian trade ministry data. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said on X that the agreement would give "fresh momentum" to India's farmers, entrepreneurs and small businesses.

What Changes for Indian Exporters

Britain will remove duties on 96.8% of tariff lines, covering 97.7% of trade by value. Tariffs of up to 70% on processed food, 21.5% on marine products, 18% on engineering goods and auto components, 16% on leather and footwear, 12% on textiles and 8% on chemicals and pharmaceuticals all drop to zero, according to India's commerce ministry.

The gem and jewellery sector stands to gain sharply. Kirit Bhansali, chairman of the Gem & Jewellery Export Promotion Council, said exports to the UK—currently around $941 million—are "poised to surge to $2.5 billion within the next three years." Engineering exporters see a similar opening: Britain is among India's top five engineering export markets, with shipments of $4.7 billion in 2025/26. EEPC chairman Pankaj Chadha told Reuters he expects that figure to exceed $7.5 billion by 2029/30.

What Changes for UK Exports to India

India will eliminate duties on 64.1% of tariff lines immediately and phase out a further 21%, while excluding sensitive products including dairy, cereals, millets and edible oils. The most symbolic concession is on Scotch whisky: duty falls from 150% to 75% immediately and to 40% over ten years. Automotive tariffs drop from over 100% to 10% under a quota system allowing 37,000 fully built vehicles a year at preferential rates. UK business secretary Peter Kyle said the deal would deliver "cuts to tariffs of £400 million within the first year alone."

Services and Mobility

The services package covers 137 sub-sectors, including IT, business services, telecommunications, finance and education, and eases temporary entry for business visitors, intra-corporate transferees, investors and independent professionals. About 1,800 Indian chefs, yoga instructors and classical musicians will receive dedicated mobility opportunities annually. The pact also opens Britain's government procurement market—estimated at £90 billion ($121 billion)—to Indian suppliers.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 1.9 million people of Indian origin in the UK, the accompanying Double Contribution Convention is perhaps the most tangible benefit. It exempts Indian professionals on temporary UK assignments from paying social security contributions in both countries for up to five years—up from three years previously. India's commerce ministry said over 75,000 workers and 900 employers will benefit directly. NRI-owned businesses in IT, healthcare and consultancy gain improved regulatory certainty, while the UK estimates the deal will increase bilateral trade by £25.5 billion annually in the long run.

What Comes Next

The deal arrives as Andy Burnham assumes office as UK Prime Minister, succeeding Sir Keir Starmer. Strategic experts expect continuity on trade, given Burnham's record of working with Indian enterprises as Mayor of Greater Manchester.

Challenges remain. India's push for a more generous mobility framework for IT professionals fell short due to immigration sensitivities in Britain. India also failed to secure relief from the UK's upcoming Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which could affect carbon-intensive exports. As ORF fellow Soumya Bhowmick wrote, the deal's real significance will be measured not in trade balances alone but in its ability to "shift the underlying geometry of trade and investment" in green technology, pharmaceuticals and digital innovation.
